<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and say to her: "These things, O Queen, I willingly suffer for you; you will restore me to wholeness, or certainly you alone are enough for me in place of all others. Cherish me in your pious bosom alone, so that I may not feel the loss of life, let alone the loss of fame."

*Sorrow.* I am torn apart everywhere in the crossroads by the common folk.

*Reason.* Take it in good part. The common folk will make you known, virtue will make you famous, and conscience will make you secure.

---

### On the shame sought from unworthy praises.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you later condemn, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the start of the response from Reason.</note>

*Reason.* An evil thing is often born from a good root. For the good and innocent imagine others to be just as they are themselves. From this, they are even more prone to praise than is fair. And although I admit it is an evil thing to praise the unworthy, to disparage the undeserving is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. To be deceived is someone else's fault; to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another turns to my infamy.

*Reason.* On the contrary, it is either your fault or your ignorance. From another person, just as there is no praise, so there is no infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve deeply that I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not grieve for this same thing often. Beware of leaping forward rashly to praise or to disparage. For there is a lust for both things and, to speak properly, a certain disease and itch of a moving tongue that knows no rest. The restraint and guarding of the tongue are numbered among the works of exceptional perfection, as the Scripture says:

<summary>Reason advises Sorrow on handling a damaged reputation and the error of praising unworthy individuals, noting that being deceived is better than deceiving others. The dialogue warns against the impulsive urge to praise or criticize, characterizing it as a lack of self-control.</summary>
<keywords>reputation, virtue, conscience, praise, gossip, integrity, self-restraint</keywords>
